High King of the Uí Néill, ancestor of one of the most enduring dynasties in Europe. From the hills of Tara, Niall looked across the sea — and reached for what lay beyond it. Take the crown, Niall. Take your hostages, and make your name echo through the ages.

Conquering a [icon:YIELD_CITIES] [TIP:LOC_PEDIA_CONCEPTS_CITIES_TOOLTIP]Settlement[/TIP] grants [B]+1 [icon:YIELD_CULTURE] Culture[/B] and [B]+1 [icon:YIELD_PRODUCTION] Production[/B] to all [icon:YIELD_CITIES] [TIP:LOC_PEDIA_CONCEPTS_CITIES_TOOLTIP]Cities[/TIP]. Stacks over the course of the Age.
Niall respects leaders who expand through force. He has little patience for those who build monuments while leaving their borders undefended.
A king does not trust. A king ensures.
The nine hostages kept their oaths, and the Uí Néill built a dominion the sea itself could not bound.
[B]Niall's[/B] war-bands raided the frontiers of [B]Rome's[/B] Britain for plunder and slaves.
[B]Greece's[/B] Mediterranean lay at the far edge of the raiding sea [B]Niall[/B] sailed.
The wealth of [B]Egypt[/B] was legend even among the kings of [B]Niall's[/B] age.

Niall of the Nine Hostages (Irish: Niall Noígíallach) was a High King of Ireland in the late fourth and early fifth century AD. He is the ancestor of the Uí Néill dynasty, which dominated Irish and Scottish politics for centuries after his death.

His sobriquet does not recall victories over nine foreign kingdoms. The nine hostages were members of Niall's own extended kin, held as political insurance so that his dynasty's internal power could not fracture. He trusted his family no further than he could compel them.

Niall's power was built on raids carried ever farther abroad. His war-bands crossed the Irish Sea into Roman Britain, returning with tribute, plunder, and slaves — the greatest returns any Irish king had yet obtained. Traditional dating places his reign from roughly 380 to 405 AD.

It was on one such raid that a Romano-British teenager named Patricius was carried into servitude in Ireland. Patrick later escaped, returned as a missionary, and set about the conversion of Ireland — a consequence Niall almost certainly never intended. The slave his captains dismissed became the architect of Irish Christianity.

The Uí Néill line held power in Ireland for five centuries, sending branches into Scotland and, far later, into the Scots-Irish diaspora of the Atlantic world. Genetic studies suggest several million men worldwide descend from Niall through the paternal line — making him one of the most successful dynasts in recorded history.

Niall died sometime between 405 and 428 AD; the circumstances are unknown. No contemporary portrait survives, and every depiction of him is imagination and convention. What remains is a dynasty, a name — and a legend the size of an island.
